quotes: At birth she presented with microcephaly and hypotonia that progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalised hypertonia by the first year of life. She never developed speech or independent walking and has been wheelchair-bound since 5 years of age, when she also started experiencing generalised tonic-clonic seizures.

A brain MRI revealed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was more pronounced in the frontal region and corpus callosum (supplementary figure 1).

We identified a 139 kb (minimum) to 222 kb (maximum) homozygous deletion of chromosome 15q21.2 that includes the 5′ end of two genes: AP4E1 (adaptor related protein complex-4, epsilon-1) and SPPL2A (signal peptide peptidase-like-2A).

notes.statement: Kong et al. (2018) reported two monozygotic twin sisters, aged 8 years, born to first-cousin Moroccan parents, who had hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous AP4E1 p.R1105X mutation in addition to Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease caused by homozygous SPPL2A mutation; neonatal asphyxiation had been noted at delivery.
quotes: No complications had been observed during the pregnancy, but neonatal asphyxiation was noted during the delivery.
In addition to MSMD, the patients displayed hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous p.R1105X mutation of the AP4E1 gene.
a family from Morocco including two affected eight-year-old monozygotic twin sisters (P1 and P2, Kindred A, Fig. 1a)

notes.statement: In identical Moroccan twins, born to first-cousin parents, with complex HSP and BCG lymphadenitis, Kong et al. (2013) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsense mutation in AP4E1 (R1105X). The parents were heterozygous, and the mutation was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls or 69 Moroccan controls.
quotes: We found only one homozygous nonsense mutation in AP4E1 (Figure 1B, Table 2), resulting in the replacement of an arginine residue in position 1105 with a premature stop codon (p.R1105X).

This variant was not found in the sequences of 1,050 healthy controls from 51 ethnic groups from the Centre d'Étude du Polymorphisme Humain (CEPH) panel [35], [36] or in an additional 69 Moroccan controls.

notes.statement: Kong et al. (2013) found that the R1105X mutation did not change AP4E1 mRNA levels in patient EBV-B cells. However, AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable, and levels of AP-4-mu and AP-4-beta were also reduced. Assembled AP-4 complex in patient fibroblasts and EBV-B cells was more than 95% lower than in controls, and the AP-4 binding partner tepsin was not detectable in patient fibroblasts.
quotes: AP-4ε was barely detectable in EBV-B cells from P1, but was clearly present in control cells (Figure 2C). In addition, the loss of AP-4ε resulted in a concomitant decrease in the levels of both the AP-4 μ and AP-4β proteins in the patient’s cells.
IMAGE J quantification indicated that AP-4 assembly levels were more than 95% lower than those of healthy controls
tepsin, which binds to the C-terminal appendage domain of AP-4β [32], was detectable in control fibroblasts, but not in those of P1 (Figure 3B)

notes.statement: Kong et al. (2013) did not identify any immunologic abnormality to explain the mycobacterial disease in the twins. Lymphocyte subsets, immunoglobulins, complement, the IL-12/IFN-gamma circuit, and oxidative burst were all normal. The authors proposed that the AP4E1 mutation was the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease. They suggested that the mutation may escape nonsense-mediated decay and produce a truncated protein.
quotes: We were therefore unable to identify any abnormal immunological phenotype able to explain directly the mycobacterial disease in the patients.

In our case, the nonsense mutation p.R1105X, which is located close to the normal translation termination codon (p.X1137), does not generate a transcript subject to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) [48].
We thus propose that the AP4E1 mutation is the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease in our patients.

notes.statement: Najmabadi et al. (2011) carried out homozygosity mapping, exon enrichment and next-generation sequencing in 136 consanguineous families from Iran and elsewhere with autosomal recessive intellectual disability. They found more mutations in 23 genes already linked to intellectual disability or related neurologic disorders, plus single, probably disease-causing variants in 50 new candidate genes.
quotes: we have now performed homozygosity mapping, exon enrichment and next-generation sequencing in 136 consanguineous families with autosomal-recessive intellectual disability from Iran and elsewhere

has revealed additional mutations in 23 genes previously implicated in intellectual disability or related neurological disorders, as well as single, probably disease-causing variants in 50 novel candidate genes

notes.statement: Using autozygosity mapping combined with Sanger sequencing of candidate genes or exome sequencing in 3 consanguineous families, Abou Jamra et al. (2011) identified one mutation in each of 3 genes encoding AP4 subunits, including a splice site mutation in AP4E1 (c.542+1_542+4delGTAA) resulting in deletion of r.421_542 and a frameshift (p.Glu181GlyfsTer20).
quotes: Using a combination of autozygosity mapping and either Sanger sequencing of candidate genes or next-generation exome sequencing, we identified one mutation in each of three genes encoding adaptor protein complex 4 (AP4) subunits

notes.statement: Abou Jamra et al. (2011) concluded that mutations in different AP4 subunit genes (AP4S1, AP4B1, AP4E1) cause a clinically recognizable syndrome due to deficiency of the AP4 complex, supporting a crucial role for AP4-mediated trafficking in brain development and function.
quotes: these results support the hypothesis that AP4-complex-mediated trafficking plays a crucial role in brain development and functioning and demonstrate the existence of a clinically recognizable syndrome due to deficiency of the AP4 complex.

notes.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) used high-resolution arrays to define the homozygous 15q21.2 deletion in the affected sibs as 192 kb, removing the 5-prime ends of AP4E1 and SPPL2A, confirmed by FISH. Although they could not completely exclude a contribution from SPPL2A deletion, they proposed that AP4E1 deficiency was the main mechanism.
quotes: used this array to define the size of the deleted region to 192 kb (chr15:48835480-49028171; hg18 genome assembly, figure 1B, C).

Although we cannot completely rule out a potential pathogenic role for SPPL2A, or that its deletion might contribute to the phenotype, we propose that AP4E1 deficiency is the main underlying genetic mechanism responsible for the clinical findings observed in our patients.

notes.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) found that the mother was a heterozygous carrier of the deletion; SNRPN methylation analysis showed biparental inheritance of chromosome 15 in the probands, so the father was inferred to be a carrier, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
quotes: FISH analysis on the mother revealed that she is a heterozygous carrier of the deletion.
confirmed the presence of both methylated and unmethylated alleles, consistent with biparental inheritance for chromosome 15. Therefore, the father is inferred to be a carrier of this deletion.

notes.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) noted the close phenotypic similarity between their AP4E1-deleted family and a family with a homozygous AP4M1 mutation. They proposed that loss of any one of the four AP-4 subunits disrupts the whole complex, causing a distinct autosomal recessive 'AP-4 deficiency syndrome'.
quotes: Two unrelated families with homozygous disruptions in different subunits (ε and μ) show extremely similar clinical phenotypes (this report and the family reported by Verkerk et al).
we propose that disruption of any one of the four subunits of AP-4 abolishes its function and causes a distinct autosomal recessive disorder that we refer to as ‘AP-4 deficiency syndrome’.
